query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting a fraction of the heavy Ta in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a lightweight element such as Al (e.g. replacing ~20–30% of Ta by atomic fraction) will reduce the overall alloy density by 5–10% while maintaining the BCC solid-solution phase and preserving the excellent room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical strengths.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr showing a homogeneous BCC solid‐solution structure with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³, a room‐temperature yield strength near 1600 MPa, and an elevated temperature (~1000 °C) yield strength of ~855 MPa.
generation.intervention: Partial compositional substitution of Ta with Al such that approximately 20–30% of the Ta content is replaced by Al.
generation.conditions: Compression tests conducted at room temperature and at 1000 °C with comparable strain rates (as in prior tests on as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr).
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the single BCC solid‐solution structure; any lattice parameter contraction induced by moderate Al addition should stimulate solid-solution strengthening without triggering deleterious intermetallic or ordered phases.
generation.mechanism: Al is a lightweight element with a small atomic radius. Its partial substitution for the heavy Ta is expected to lower the overall density while maintaining complete solubility in the BCC matrix if added in modest amounts. The induced lattice contraction (and attendant increased lattice distortion) can preserve—or even slightly enhance—the dislocation resistance at room and high temperatures by maintaining effective solid-solution strengthening. This balance is critical, since excessive substitution has been seen to compromise ductility; moderate Ta replacement by Al should avoid that pitfall by keeping the beneficial contributions of Hf and Mo to high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a density reduction of roughly 5–10% relative to as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr, with room‐temperature yield strength and 1000 °C yield strength maintained within ±5–10% of baseline values. Ductility should remain acceptable (losses not exceeding 10%) so that the alloy’s overall performance is preserved.
generation.baseline: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with density ~10.21 g/cm³, ~1600 MPa RT yield strength, and ~855 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Intervention effectiveness is assessed only as long as the addition does not provoke phase separation, formation of brittle intermetallics, or undue loss of ductility. Tests are constrained to room temperature and 1000 °C under quasi-static compressive loading.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines evidence that lightweight element additions can reduce density and alter solid-solution strengthening (PMC8746096 and PMC8074761) with the baseline performance data for as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr (PMC7514121). What is new here is the targeted substitution of Ta (rather than Hf) with Al to lower density while preserving the synergistic role of Hf in high-temperature strength; however, the optimal substitution level and possible subtle effects on ductility and phase stability remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of alloys with a fixed composition of HfMoTaTiZr in which Ta is progressively replaced by Al in increments (e.g., 0%, 20%, 30%, 40% substitution by atomic fraction). Ensure identical as-cast processing conditions to maintain the BCC single-phase microstructure. Evaluate microstructure (via XRD, SEM/EDS) and mechanical properties.
measurements: XRD to confirm phase retention and absence of deleterious intermetallic phases
Room temperature and 1000 °C compressive yield strength (and ductility) using standard compression tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with 20–30% Ta substitution by Al does not achieve at least a 5% reduction in density relative to the baseline, or if its room-temperature or 1000 °C yield strength decreases by more than 15% relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if excessive brittle phases or intermetallics form, then the hypothesis that Ta substitution by Al can reduce density without sacrificing mechanical performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. AbstractSingle-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been receiving significant attention due to their excellent mechanical properties and phase stability at elevated temperatures. Recently, many studies have been reported regarding the precipitation-enhanced alloy design strategy to further improve the mechanical properties of RHEAs at elevated temperatures. In this study, we attempted to develop precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs via addition of Ni or Co into Al0.8NbTiV HEA. The added elements were selected due to their smaller atomic radius and larger mixing enthalpy, which is known to stimulate the formation of precipitates. The addition of the Ni or Co leads to the formation of the sigma precipitates with homogeneous distribution. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in improvement of yield strength. Furthermore, the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) HEAs show excellent specific yield strength compared to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718) at elevated temperatures.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory alloys, lightweight, sigma phase, mech

Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
